clue.text: Kipling's regimental superior

parts.note: Kipling's poem about an Indian water-carrier ends with the soldier telling him he is a better man than the speaker, so this humble regimental servant is called his superior

explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's poem the narrator, a British soldier, ends by admitting the water-carrier who saved him is 'a better man than I am', so 'superior' means morally better, not higher in rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Kipling's ballad is a regimental water-bearer whom the soldier-narrator admits is the better man.

clue.text: Grand extent of Mariana's moated dwelling

parts.note: a range is a spread or extent

explanation.surface: A description of the grand size of a literary heroine's moated house.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's poem 'Mariana' places her 'in the moated grange', a quotation from Shakespeare's Measure for Measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's Mariana waits forlornly in a farmhouse estate surrounded by a moat, the 'moated grange'.

clue.text: Medicine all gone lumpy?

parts.note: when something is all gone there is none, NO
a dose is a measure of medicine

explanation.surface: A patient finds the medicine finished and wonders if it has gone lumpy.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's order is DOSE then NO, but read as 'no dose' the medicine is all gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Nodose is a botanical and medical term for knotty, full of nodes or swellings.

clue.text: Outlook for an air-navigator in Houston

definitions.text: Outlook for an air-navigator in Houston

parts.words: Outlook for an air-navigator in Houston
parts.note: an aircraft's navigator once took star sightings through a transparent dome in the roof, and Houston's famous covered stadium bears the same name

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses are blended: the perspex bubble on an aircraft used for celestial navigation, and the domed baseball stadium in Houston, Texas.
explanation.definitionFit: A transparent roof bubble on an aircraft lets the navigator sight stars; Houston's indoor stadium took the name too.

clue.text: Do students dip into it for "unseen "" translations ?

definitions.text: Do students dip into it for "unseen "" translations ?

parts.words: Do students dip into it for "unseen "" translations ?
parts.note: an unseen is a passage set for translation at sight in a language class; here the pen is dipped into a writing fluid whose marks cannot be seen

explanation.walkthrough: An 'unseen' is a British school exam passage translated without preparation; the clue pretends students dip into a reference book, but they dip a pen into a fluid that leaves invisible writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing fluid that leaves no visible trace until heated or treated is the secret-writing medium of spies.

clue.text: Bert is worried by racial divisions

indicators.note: being worried suggests being shaken up and agitated, so the letters before it are reworked

explanation.surface: A man named Bert is troubled by ethnic divisions in society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' does two things in the surface, but in the parse it is fodder alongside BERT, with 'worried' as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tribes are groups of people sharing descent, the old sense of racial or ethnic subdivisions.

clue.text: Boy with party piece of music

parts.note: Ron is a boy's name
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A young man brings a musical number along to a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form in which a main theme keeps returning between contrasting episodes.

clue.text: Lines acknowledging a poet

parts.note: BR stands for British Rail, whose railway lines are 'lines'
owning up to something is acknowledging it

explanation.surface: Some verses written as a tribute to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' suggests lines of verse to suit the poet, but it is BR, British Rail, the old UK railway network.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Browning was a major Victorian poet, author of 'My Last Duchess'.

clue.text: Superlative hours Burns spent among the lasses

definitions.text: Superlative hours Burns spent among the lasses

parts.words: Superlative hours Burns spent among the lasses
parts.note: Robert Burns's song 'Green Grow the Rashes' says the most delightful hours he ever spends are spent among the lasses

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet, wrote 'The sweetest hours that e'er I spend / Are spent among the lasses, O'; 'Superlative' asks for the -est form of the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in Burns's line is in its superlative degree, the most delightful.

clue.text: A divine vermouth I have as an extra ingredient

parts.note: a divine is a clergyman, and DD is Doctor of Divinity
IT is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it
contracted to I've

explanation.surface: A clergyman adds his vermouth to a drink as an extra flavouring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin and it' is a British cocktail of gin and Italian (sweet) vermouth, hence IT for vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: An additive is a substance added to food or fuel to improve it, an extra component.

clue.text: Again abroad for an unoriginal performance

explanation.surface: A call for a repeated performance heard overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: In French the word means 'again', and an audience calls it to get a repeat of a number already performed.

clue.text: Mad Fred has fun with shire deputy officer

indicators.note: something mad is crazed and disordered, so the letters that follow are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A crazy man called Fred has a good time with a county's officials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'with' only join the three pieces of fodder FRED, FUN and SHIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: An under-sheriff is the official who acts as a sheriff's assistant and stands in for him.

clue.text: Keen enjoyment of a bit of wind, nothing more

parts.note: a gust is a brief burst of wind
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone takes great pleasure in a mere breath of wind and nothing else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'more' simply says the O comes on top of, after, GUST.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusto is hearty relish or zest in doing something.

clue.text: Top cover-up with a shady project

definitions.text: Top cover-up with a shady project

parts.words: Top cover-up with a shady project
parts.note: a hat worn on the top of the head, with a brim that projects to give shade from the sun, read as if it were a dubious scheme to conceal something

explanation.walkthrough: 'cover-up' and 'shady project' suggest a scandal, but the shady project is a brim sticking out to give shade.
explanation.definitionFit: A brimmed bonnet worn to shield the face and neck from strong light is a head covering with a projecting shade.

clue.text: Horse takes happily endowed ones on the road

definitions.note: a phrase describing where the plural noun is found, the paving of an old street

parts.note: a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse
to be blest is to be fortunately gifted

explanation.surface: A horse picks up lucky travellers along the highway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' joins the pieces; 'ones' plays double duty in the surface, but the definition is the description 'on the road', meaning what is laid on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rounded stones once used to pave streets form the surface of old roads.

clue.text: The MS in full

parts.note: MS looks like the abbreviation for manuscript or multiple sclerosis, but read as several Roman numeral Ms, each worth 1000, written out in words

explanation.walkthrough: MS is read as the plural of M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, and 'in full' asks for it spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: M is the Roman numeral for one thousand, so several Ms spelt out become a plural count of thousands.

clue.text: Prohibition not in time to make the columns

parts.note: tabu is a variant spelling of taboo, a prohibition
late means not on time

explanation.surface: A ban came too late for something to make the newspaper columns.
explanation.definitionFit: To tabulate is to arrange data in a table of rows and columns.

clue.text: Detectives in training?

parts.note: people who watch out for and note things are detectives of a sort, and those who do it at railway stations are ...; 'in training' hides that compound

explanation.walkthrough: 'in training' suggests apprentices, but read it as 'in train-ing': the hobbyists who note locomotive numbers are trainspotters.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotters are people who look out for and identify things, like trainspotters or aircraft spotters.

clue.text: In how like a god! (Hamlet)

parts.note: the clue quotes Hamlet's speech on man with one word left out after 'In'

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says of man: 'in action how like an angel! in apprehension how like a god!'; the clue is a fill-in-the-blank quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Here the word means understanding or grasp, the mental faculty that makes man seem godlike in Hamlet's speech.

clue.text: Girl may be all set for stardom

indicators.note: says the letters of the words that follow may be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A young woman may be all ready to become a star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for stardom' adds a hint: the name is Latin for star.
explanation.definitionFit: Stella is a woman's name, from the Latin word for star.

clue.text: Beach-protector gives Lady Jane no trouble

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: Lady Jane Grey was queen of England for nine days in 1553

explanation.surface: A sea defence causes a noblewoman no difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' reads as a noun after 'no', as if the lady had no difficulty, but it is the anagram signal. Lady Jane Grey was the 'nine days queen' of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A groyne is a low wall built out from the shore to stop sand and shingle being washed away.

clue.text: Nature, etc, reproduced in speech

indicators.note: reproduced suggests the letters are produced again in a different form

explanation.surface: Nature and so on, repeated in what someone says.
explanation.definitionFit: An utterance is something spoken, a vocal expression.

clue.text: Like the day of economic depression

definitions.text: Like the day of economic depression

parts.words: Like the day of economic depression
parts.note: the saying about putting money by for hard times names a wet sort of day

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'saving for a rainy day' means keeping money for a time of hardship; 'depression' also suggests low-pressure weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Wet weather days stand for times of hardship in the saying about saving money for one.

clue.text: In many ways a tyrant is a beastly lecher

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow, spanning the join between them

explanation.surface: In many respects a despot is a brutish womaniser.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'wayS A TYRant'.
explanation.definitionFit: A satyr is a goat-legged woodland creature of Greek myth, given to lust, and so a lewd man.

clue.text: Girl identifies herself with a writer of 26

parts.note: she says 'I am', so AM
Elia was the pen name of Charles Lamb, author of essays (the answer to 26)

explanation.surface: A young woman claims to be one with a famous author.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb wrote the 'Essays of Elia'; 26 across is ESSAYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Amelia is a woman's name, and the title of Fielding's novel.

clue.text: Engage helper in remarkable manner

parts.note: to sign someone is to engage them under contract
an ally is a supporter or helper

explanation.surface: Taking on an assistant in an unusual way.
explanation.definitionFit: Signally means notably or conspicuously.

clue.text: Experimental literature

definitions.meaning: attempts or trials, an experimental sense of the word
short prose compositions on a subject form a genre of writing

explanation.definitionFit: The word means trial attempts (from French essayer, to try) and also short prose compositions.

clue.text: How actors disappear and coach passengers appear

explanation.surface: Actors exit while travellers step down from a coach.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors exit out of the audience's sight into the wings, and passengers alight from a horse-drawn coach.
